stem.text: The diagram shows a section of an addition polymer.

stem.alt: Displayed formula of a section of a polymer chain of six carbon atoms joined by single bonds, with continuation bonds at both ends. Each carbon carries one H atom and one Cl atom: the Cl atoms alternate above and below the chain (Cl up on carbons 1, 3 and 5, Cl down on carbons 2, 4 and 6).

stem.text: What is the name of this polymer?

explanation.text: Every carbon in the chain has one H and one Cl, so the repeat unit is two carbons long: –CHCl–CHCl–. Putting the C=C back between those two carbons gives the monomer CHCl=CHCl, 1,2-dichloroethene.
An addition polymer is named after its monomer, which must be an alkene. The polymer itself contains only C–C single bonds, but the name keeps the “-ene” of the monomer.

optionAnalysis.text: Names the polymer after the saturated repeat unit; 1,2-dichloroethane has no C=C and could not undergo addition polymerisation.
Repeat unit –CHCl–CHCl– comes from the monomer CHCl=CHCl, 1,2-dichloroethene.
Takes a three-carbon repeat unit, and propane has no C=C to polymerise.
1,2,3-trichloropropene is CHCl=CCl–CH<sub>2</sub>Cl; its polymer would carry a CH<sub>2</sub>Cl side group on every other chain carbon, but the chain shown has no side groups.

reasoningChain: Each chain carbon carries H and Cl: the smallest repeating unit is –CHCl–CHCl–.

inferredMistakes.text: Naming the polymer after the saturated repeat unit (an “-ane”) instead of the alkene monomer.
Choosing a three-carbon repeat unit because the section shows six carbons.
